items.title: Distinguish DNA packaging terms
items.guide: Chromatin is DNA with associated proteins. A chromosome is an organized DNA molecule/protein structure. After replication, one chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at a centromeric region; after separation each chromatid is counted as a daughter chromosome. Chromosome number and DNA amount are different quantities.
items.bindingReview: Chromatin packaging versus chromosome unit versus sister-copy relationship; separated chromatids become daughter chromosomes.

items.title: Explain interphase
items.guide: G1 supports growth and normal activity; S replicates DNA; G2 prepares for division and checks readiness. DNA amount doubles in S while chromosome number, counted by centromeres before separation, stays the same. Interphase is active rather than a resting stage.
items.bindingReview: G1 activity/growth, S replication, G2 preparation; no ploidy doubling or resting-stage claim.

items.title: Label early mitosis
items.guide: A points to a duplicated chromosome, B to spindle fibres, and C to the breaking-down nuclear envelope. Explain condensation and spindle development. The figure is a model, so a precise drawing should distinguish centromere/kinetochore attachment from a spindle attaching anywhere on DNA.
items.bindingReview: Source drawing re-viewed: A duplicated chromosome, B spindle fibres, C disrupted envelope; attachment mechanism belongs at kinetochore.

items.title: Explain chromosome reduction
items.guide: Gametes normally contain one chromosome set. Fertilization joins two sets and restores the diploid number. Without reduction, fusion would double chromosome number each generation. This is a set-count argument, not a claim that gametes contain fewer kinds of essential genes.
items.bindingReview: Reduction before fertilization prevents repeated set doubling; gametes retain one set.

items.title: Match divisions to life-cycle context
items.guide: Tissue renewal and embryo growth normally use mitosis. Human gamete formation uses meiosis, but plant gametes form by mitosis in haploid gametophytes after meiosis has produced spores. The unqualified phrase “production of gametes” therefore needs an organism/life-cycle context.
items.bindingReview: Tissue/embryonic mitosis and animal meiotic gametogenesis contrasted with haploid plant gametophyte mitosis.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: State the life-cycle context: not all organisms form gametes directly by meiosis.

items.title: Choose a tissue for observation
items.guide: A growing root or shoot meristem supplies many mitotically dividing plant cells. Meiotic cells occur in reproductive structures such as anthers or ovules at the appropriate developmental stage. The local course uses supplied observations; choosing a tissue does not demonstrate slide preparation or microscope operation.
items.bindingReview: Actively dividing versus spore-forming tissue and development stage; optional meristem/anther/ovule context precedes attempt.
items.preAttemptContext: A meristem is a region of actively dividing plant cells, such as a growing root or shoot tip. In flowering plants, spore-producing cells in anthers and ovules undergo meiosis at suitable developmental stages. The resulting haploid generation later produces gametes by mitosis.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Locate replication
items.guide: DNA replication occurs during S phase of interphase, before mitosis or meiosis I. There is no second full S phase between meiosis I and II. Replication doubles DNA copies without doubling chromosome sets.
items.bindingReview: S precedes nuclear divisions and is absent between meiosis I/II.

items.title: Identify metaphase I
items.guide: The right-hand diagram represents homologous pairs positioned together for the first meiotic division. Use pairing of homologues, rather than just the presence of X shapes, as the deciding evidence. X-shaped duplicated chromosomes can also appear in mitosis.
items.bindingReview: Viewed right diagram has homologues paired, unlike individually aligned left chromosomes; X shape alone is insufficient.

items.title: Count after the first meiotic division
items.guide: Each product is haploid because it has one homologue from each original pair. Its chromosomes are still duplicated, with sister chromatids attached. “Haploid” refers to sets, not to whether a chromosome has one or two chromatids.
items.bindingReview: One homologue per pair with sisters joined gives haploid duplicated products.

items.title: Qualify crossing-over language
items.guide: Routine meiotic crossing over occurs between nonsister chromatids during homologous synapsis in prophase I. Ordinary mitosis lacks that programmed pairing/exchange sequence and usually preserves daughter-cell genetic similarity. The source’s absolute “does not occur” is too strong: mitotic recombination can occur, so do not teach it as impossible.
items.bindingReview: Routine meiotic synapsis/crossing over differs from ordinary mitosis; rare mitotic recombination not ruled out.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Distinguish ordinary meiotic crossing over from the possibility of mitotic recombination.

items.title: Count chromosomes and copies
items.guide: Fruit fly after meiosis I: 4 duplicated chromosomes per product. Pea after meiosis II: 7 unduplicated chromosomes. Frog somatic interphase: 26 chromosomes, but duplication depends on whether the cell is before, during or after S; “interphase” alone is insufficient. Pine gametophyte in mitotic prophase: 12 duplicated chromosomes.
items.bindingReview: Four table rows independently counted: fly4 duplicated, pea7 unduplicated, frog26 with S-stage ambiguity, haploid pine12 duplicated.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Interphase includes before, during and after replication. The frog row needs a specified interphase stage before its duplication state can be determined.

items.title: Compare the two division sequences
items.guide: The upper sequence is mitosis: one division separates sister chromatids and preserves chromosome-set number in two cells. The lower is meiosis: homologues separate first, then sisters, producing four haploid products in this model. Label what separates at each division and distinguish one replication from two divisions.
items.bindingReview: Viewed upper mitotic one-division/two-product and lower two-division/four-product model; count sets and structures separated.

items.title: Reason about timing and exposure
items.guide: Early development often has rapidly dividing, differentiating tissues, so the same specified exposure can affect major developmental processes more strongly than in a later-stage organism. Effects still depend on dose, tissue and timing. The comparison is a biological risk mechanism, not a certain prediction for an individual.
items.bindingReview: Developmental sensitivity context is explicit before optional comparison; no individual deterministic risk.
items.preAttemptContext: Optional developmental context: early embryonic tissues divide, differentiate and establish major body patterns. Damage during a sensitive stage can affect many later descendants or the formation of structures. The comparison must specify exposure, tissue and timing; age alone cannot determine an individual outcome.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Test a cell-cycle hypothesis
items.guide: Shortened interphase, particularly growth/checkpoint intervals, is a plausible hypothesis; total cycle time alone cannot identify the shortened phase. A proposed digital study would need time-stamped cell sequences from comparable reference and altered-regulation populations, suitable phase markers, a stage-classification guide, a computer and a results table. Define the stage rules, hold recording intervals and conditions comparable, follow many cells through complete cycles, record phase durations and cell losses, then compare repeated samples. Ordinary morphology alone may not distinguish G1 from S or G2, so that narrower hypothesis needs additional phase evidence. This is a study design, not proof that all cancer cells cycle faster or that the required time-lapse data are already supplied.
items.bindingReview: Hypothesis, comparison procedure and materials now all explicit; phase evidence limits and unsupplied proposed dataset status clear.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed missing procedure/materials or explicit feature list.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Shortened interphase or altered checkpoints are plausible explanations for a faster cycle, but total cycle time does not identify a phase by itself. Plan repeated time-lapse observations of comparable cell populations, classify stages with a consistent rule, and compare their durations. Do not treat all cancer cells as uniformly faster or infer a diagnosis.

items.title: Predict incorrect chromosome pairing
items.guide: Pairing or exchange between nonhomologous regions can misalign genes and create rearrangements or unbalanced products. Explain the normal need for corresponding homologous regions. The consequence depends on where the error occurs; do not claim every such event produces the same syndrome.
items.bindingReview: Corresponding-region alignment needed to avoid unbalanced exchange, no fixed syndrome inferred.

items.title: Draw alternating generations
items.guide: Show diploid sporophyte → meiosis → haploid spores → mitosis → haploid gametophyte → mitosis → gametes → fertilization → diploid zygote → mitosis → sporophyte. Three key features are two multicellular generations of different ploidy; meiosis reducing sets and fertilization restoring them; and spores developing without fusion while gametes fuse. This plant cycle differs from merely alternating sexual and asexual modes in an animal.
items.bindingReview: Full cycle includes mitotic zygote growth and three separately stated distinctive features.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed missing procedure/materials or explicit feature list.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Show diploid sporophyte → meiosis → haploid spores → mitosis → haploid gametophyte → mitosis → gametes → fertilization → diploid zygote → sporophyte. Mark ploidy and the two transitions. Spores develop without fusion; gametes fuse. This plant cycle differs from simply alternating sexual and asexual reproduction in an animal.

items.title: Explain segregation
items.guide: The two alleles at a locus separate into different gametes as homologous chromosomes segregate in meiosis. Each normal gamete receives one allele copy. Fertilization restores a pair; allele separation does not destroy the recessive allele.
items.bindingReview: Allele segregation connected to homologous separation and restoration at fertilization.

items.title: Use a stated dominant-trait model
items.guide: Treat the eyelid example as a fictional complete-dominance model, not a universal human trait rule. A dominant phenotype may be DD or Dd. Dd × dd predicts half Dd and half dd. Three recessive-phenotype children are possible by chance from Dd × dd, with probability (1/2)³=1/8; they are impossible from DD × dd under this simplified model.
items.bindingReview: DD/Dd possibilities, Dd×dd half each and three recessive outcomes1/8 independently recomputed; fictional trait assumption retained.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Use the stipulated fictional one-locus model; do not present the human eyelid trait as a universal Mendelian characteristic.

items.title: Separate conditional and joint probabilities
items.guide: For Aa × Aa, each child has probability 1/4 of aa under the stated model. Before either birth, two specified aa outcomes have joint probability 1/16. Once the first child’s outcome is known, the second remains an independent 1/4 event; it does not become 1/16.
items.bindingReview: Known first birth leaves next probability1/4; two future specified events would give1/16.

items.title: Interpret incomplete dominance
items.guide: Use alleles P and W with PW lavender. PP × WW gives all PW in F1. PW × PW predicts 1 PP:2 PW:1 WW, with matching purple:lavender:white phenotypes. The observed 28:52:19 is a sample of 99, not an exact ratio; incomplete dominance explains the intermediate heterozygote without blending away alleles.
items.bindingReview: PP×WW gives allPW; F1cross1:2:1 and observed99 not exactpredictions; no blendedallele.

items.title: Explain a test cross
items.guide: Cross an individual showing the dominant phenotype but unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive partner. A heterozygote predicts both phenotypes, whereas a homozygous dominant predicts only dominant offspring under the model. A finite all-dominant sample supports but does not prove homozygosity.
items.bindingReview: Recessive tester reveals recessive contribution; finite all-dominant sample not conclusive.

items.title: Interpret two mouse crosses
items.guide: Let G be dominant grey and g recessive albino. The female is gg. The second grey male must be Gg because albino offspring occur. The first grey male could be GG or Gg; six grey offspring make GG plausible but do not prove it. Any grey offspring from a gg mother is Gg, so the stated later grey × grey cross predicts 3 grey:1 albino.
items.bindingReview: ggmother, secondGgfather, firstGGorGg; both selectedgreyoffspring necessarilyGg, final3:1.

items.title: Calculate ABO alternatives
items.guide: A type-B parent may be IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi. With IᴬIᴮ, IᴮIᴮ predicts half B and half AB. Iᴮi predicts 1/4 A,1/2 B,1/4 AB. No O child is possible in this simple ABO model because the AB parent has no i allele. An A child would establish that the B parent contributed i.
items.bindingReview: Both possible paternalBgenotypes enumerated; A child requires paternal i, O impossible withABmother.

items.title: Infer possible ABO genotypes
items.guide: An AB child needs Iᴬ and Iᴮ, one from each parent. With an AB mother, the father can be IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi, IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi or IᴬIᴮ. A type-O ii father cannot supply either allele. Compatibility does not establish parentage.
items.bindingReview: Five A/B/AB paternalgenotypes compatible; ii excluded, compatibility notproofidentity.

items.title: Trace a Y-linked model
items.guide: Under the stated Y-linked mechanism, a female offspring does not receive the paternal Y and therefore cannot transmit that Y-linked allele to a son. The model probability is zero through that daughter. State the chromosome route rather than generalizing to every sex-influenced trait.
items.bindingReview: PaternalY not transmitted through daughter, zero under statedYroute.

items.title: Explain a dihybrid pattern
items.guide: One model for the picture uses Y/y for yellow/green and R/r for round/wrinkled, with complete dominance and true-breeding starting parents YYRR × yyrr. Their F1 offspring are YyRr. Independent assortment gives YR, Yr, yR and yr gametes, each with probability 1/4. Crossing the F1 predicts 9 yellow-round:3 green-round:3 yellow-wrinkled:1 green-wrinkled. The new combinations illustrate assortment of the two traits under this model. The four pictures are categories, not observed counts or four equally likely outcomes, so the picture alone does not verify the numerical ratio.
items.bindingReview: Viewed pea diagram and independently derived true-breeding/double-heterozygote model; actual fourcategories notratioevidence.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed explicit cross assumptions, denominators and discriminating procedures.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: The image illustrates two traits producing new combinations after an F1 cross. Under complete dominance and independent assortment, a double-heterozygote cross predicts four phenotype categories in a 9:3:3:1 ratio. The four pictures are categories, not four equally likely outcomes or observed counts.

items.title: Account for a lethal genotype
items.guide: Platinum individuals are Pp; PP is lethal under the supplied model. Pp × Pp predicts 1/4 PP,1/2 Pp,1/4 pp at conception. Among surviving offspring, the expected ratio is 2 platinum:1 silver. A true-breeding viable platinum PP line cannot be established under these assumptions.
items.bindingReview: Conception1:2:1 becomes survivor2:1; viable true-breedingPP impossible under lethalmodel.

items.title: Calculate an X-linked cross
items.guide: Use Xᴺ for the stated normal allele and Xᶜ for the recessive colour-vision allele. The mother is XᴺXᶜ because her father was affected; the unaffected father is XᴺY. His own father supplied Y rather than his X-linked allele. No daughter is affected under the model because all inherit his Xᴺ. Assuming an equal probability of a boy or girl, a boy with normal vision has probability 1/2×1/2=1/4 of all births, or 1/2 conditional on being a boy.
items.bindingReview: Motherobligatecarrier, fatherunaffectedXNY despitehisaffectedfather; daughter0 and boynormal1/4 with equal-sex assumption.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed explicit cross assumptions, denominators and discriminating procedures.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Use Xᴺ for the stated normal allele and Xᶜ for the recessive colour-vision allele. The mother is XᴺXᶜ because her father was affected; the unaffected father is XᴺY. An affected girl has probability 0 in this model. A boy with normal vision has probability 1/4 of all births, or 1/2 conditional on being a boy.

items.title: Test a sex-associated pattern
items.guide: Only males showing the trait is compatible with Y linkage, but unspecified counts and maternal genotypes leave X-linked recessive inheritance, sex-limited expression and sampling as alternatives. To test whether females can express or transmit the trait, a proposed cross could mate a normal F1 daughter with an affected male and classify many offspring by sex. Under a simple X-linked recessive hypothesis, that daughter inherited an affected X from her father and is a carrier; the cross predicts half the daughters and half the sons affected. Under a strictly Y-linked hypothesis, no daughter inherits the allele while sons inherit the father’s Y. Record genotypes where available and compare reciprocal crosses and repeated samples. New crosses test descendant outcomes; they cannot retroactively change the already observed F1 females.
items.bindingReview: Completed discriminatingcross and predictions; male-onlyF1 doesnotuniquelyidentifylinkage, newcrossdoesnotalterexistingfemales.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: The source gives no offspring counts or maternal genotypes. A new cross can test female transmission/expression in descendants; it cannot change the already observed F1 outcomes.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed explicit cross assumptions, denominators and discriminating procedures.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Only males showing the trait is consistent with Y linkage, but absent counts and parental genotypes prevent a unique conclusion; sex-limited expression is another possibility. Compare crosses with documented genotypes and reciprocal directions. If the trait were strictly Y-linked, daughters could neither inherit nor transmit it. A proposed X-linked recessive model must also explain the actual parental and daughter outcomes.

items.title: Predict linkage evidence
items.guide: Closely linked loci can produce an excess of parental combinations and a departure from the independent 9:3:3:1 F2 prediction. A possible hypothesis is that the genes share a chromosome and usually travel together, with occasional crossing over separating them. Test a phase-known AB/ab individual against ab/ab, classify all offspring and compare parental AB/ab combinations with Ab/aB recombinants. Independence predicts four equal classes; close linkage predicts fewer recombinant offspring in this test cross. Calculate recombinants/total and check sampling, viability and scoring; multiple exchanges can hide some recombination.
items.bindingReview: Allthree requested results/hypothesis/test operations explicit; phase-known parentalclasses and numericalnull1:1:1:1.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed explicit cross assumptions, denominators and discriminating procedures.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Closely linked loci would tend to produce parental combinations more often than independent assortment predicts. Test a double heterozygote against a double recessive, classify all offspring and calculate recombinants/total. Fewer recombinants supports linkage; sample variation and multiple crossovers limit a map estimate.

items.title: Infer a dominant polled model
items.guide: Under a single-locus complete-dominance model, two polled parents producing horned calves are consistent with Pp × Pp, where P is polled. The expected phenotype ratio is 3:1, but five offspring need not match it exactly. This is an inference under stated assumptions, not proof from a small count alone.
items.bindingReview: Pp×Pp fits polledparents/hornedoffspring; three/two smallsample neednotexact3:1.

items.title: Solve the supplied pedigree
items.guide: For this fictional diagram, a recessive model fits unaffected parents producing affected daughters: use aa for shaded individuals. I-2=aa; II-2,II-3,II-4,II-5=Aa; II-1=Aa; III-2 and III-3=aa. I-1 and III-1/III-4 may be AA or Aa. The diagram’s model must not be taught as the universal inheritance pattern of osteogenesis imperfecta; real forms vary.
items.bindingReview: Pedigreeimage re-viewed: shadedI2/III2/III3aa; II1–5Aa; I1/III1/III4AAorAa. Simplifiedrecessivemodel fits, realOIinheritance notuniversal.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Solve the supplied fictional pedigree under its model. It is not a universal inheritance claim about osteogenesis imperfecta.

items.title: Explain the phage experiment
items.guide: Hershey and Chase prepared separate phage samples with radioactive phosphorus labelling DNA and radioactive sulfur labelling protein. They allowed infection of bacteria, agitated the mixtures to detach external phage coats, and separated bacterial cells from the surrounding material. Much of the DNA-associated label followed the bacterial fraction and subsequent phage production, while most protein-associated label remained outside the cells. This controlled comparison supported DNA as the hereditary material delivered in that phage system; it did not by itself establish every genetic mechanism.
items.bindingReview: All steps and measured contrast now explicit, including separation and where labels went; chemical label basis supplied before optional attempt.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed actual experimental steps and observations.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Hershey and Chase labelled phage DNA with radioactive phosphorus and protein with radioactive sulfur, let phages infect bacteria, then separated attached coats from cells. The different locations of the labels supported DNA as the transmitted hereditary material in that system. Explain the controlled comparison rather than claiming one experiment established every genetic mechanism.

items.preAttemptContext: For the label comparison, DNA contains phosphorus in its phosphate backbone and lacks sulfur. Sulfur in suitable amino-acid residues can label phage protein. Separate labelled samples allow researchers to follow these two molecular components through the same infection procedure.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: State base-ratio evidence
items.guide: For ordinary double-stranded DNA, A approximately equals T and G approximately equals C, while overall base composition differs among species. This challenged a simple repeating equal-four-base model and constrained structural explanations. The rule does not require A=G or apply unchanged to every single-stranded viral genome.
items.bindingReview: A≈T/G≈C and between-species composition reject equal-four-base repetition; not A=G or universal single-strand rule.
items.preAttemptContext: One early proposal treated DNA as a simple repeating combination with equal amounts of all four bases. A useful structural model had to account for both paired base ratios and differences in total base composition among species.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Draw directional DNA
items.guide: Draw sugar-phosphate backbones with opposite 5′/3′ directions and bases facing inward. Pair A with T and G with C, distinguishing base-pair interactions from covalent backbone bonds. Use a consistent nucleotide symbol and explain that base order, not a different backbone for each gene, carries sequence information.
items.bindingReview: Nucleotide units, external covalent backbones, internal pairs and opposite direction labels match required structural constraints.

items.title: State the missing orientation assumption
items.guide: If the supplied strand is 5′-TTCGAATCGA-3′, the aligned complement is 3′-AAGCTTAGCT-5′. Written in the conventional 5′→3′ direction, the complement is 5′-TCGATTCGAA-3′. Because the printed strand lacks orientation, state your assumption instead of presenting an unlabelled sequence.
items.bindingReview: Independently complemented TTCGAATCGA→AAGCTTAGCT aligned, then reversed TCGATTCGAA for5prime display; omitted source orientation explicitly assumed.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Strand directions are missing. State your assumed 5′/3′ orientation before writing a complement.

items.title: Explain bidirectional copying
items.guide: At each fork, DNA polymerase extends new DNA only 5′→3′. The leading strand is synthesized continuously toward fork movement; the lagging strand is made as short 5′→3′ fragments that are later joined. Two forks can move away from an origin, so fork movement and strand-synthesis direction must be labelled separately.
items.bindingReview: Bidirectional fork movement distinct from5prime-to3prime synthesis on each continuous/discontinuous strand.

items.title: Correct and order enzyme actions
items.guide: First helicase unwinds/separates paired strands; it does not cleave the sugar-phosphate backbone like a restriction enzyme. Primase makes an RNA primer, DNA polymerase extends DNA, primers are removed/replaced, and ligase seals remaining backbone nicks. The source’s “helicases cleave DNA” wording needs correction.
items.bindingReview: Unwind then prime then extend then complete joining; helicase doesnotcutbackbone and ligase seals ratherthan selects bases.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Helicase separates the strands; it does not cut the sugar-phosphate backbone.

items.title: Distinguish translation terms
items.guide: A codon is a three-base mRNA unit specifying an amino acid or stop in the reading frame. A tRNA anticodon pairs with a codon and helps deliver the associated amino acid. The ribosome positions these molecules and catalyzes peptide-bond formation. Do not call a tRNA anticodon an mRNA codon.
items.bindingReview: mRNAcodon/tRNAanticodon/ribosome roles and correct molecular boundaries.

items.title: Compare RNA roles
items.guide: mRNA carries the sequence read in translation. tRNA acts as an adaptor between a codon and an amino acid. rRNA forms major structural/catalytic parts of the ribosome. These are functional categories; RNA is not simply a disposable copy of DNA with no other roles.
items.bindingReview: mRNA information, tRNA adaptor and rRNA structural/catalytic roles all compared.

items.title: Explain restriction enzymes
items.guide: A restriction endonuclease recognizes a specified DNA sequence and cuts the backbone at defined positions. Predictable recognition permits reproducible fragments; some enzymes produce complementary overhangs useful for matching fragments. Not all restriction enzymes produce sticky ends, and cutting does not insert a gene by itself.
items.bindingReview: Sequence-specific reproducible cuts and some compatible overhangs are the two useful features; not every enzyme sticky.

items.title: Separate cutting from joining
items.guide: Restriction enzymes would still be useful for fragment analysis and mapping without ligase. Constructing stable joined DNA in the usual assembly method would be impaired because ligase seals backbone nicks. Distinguish analytical cutting from producing a complete recombinant construct.
items.bindingReview: Analysis/mapping stillpossiblewithoutligation, stable usualconstruct assembly impaired.

items.title: Explain different tissues with shared DNA
items.guide: Most nucleated somatic cells share broadly the same inherited genome, but express different sets of genes and produce different RNAs/proteins. Regulation and developmental signals help create distinct cell functions. “All cells” is a simplification: gametes, cells without nuclei and somatic sequence changes are important qualifications.
items.bindingReview: Sharedgenome with differentialexpression/processing; gametes,nucleusloss,somaticvariation qualify allcells claim.

items.title: Define the cell cycle
items.guide: The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of cell growth, DNA replication and preparation during interphase, followed by nuclear division and usually cytokinesis. Some cells leave the dividing cycle. A sequence diagram should distinguish cell activity, DNA amount and chromosome-set number.
items.bindingReview: Ordered interphase/nuclear/cytoplasmic events, with possible cell-cycle exit and set/copy distinction.

items.title: Order mitosis
items.guide: Prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase. Connect each name to observable evidence: condensation/spindle development, alignment, sister separation, and nuclear reformation. Cytokinesis is related but distinct and can overlap later mitotic events.
items.bindingReview: Prophase→metaphase→anaphase→telophase plus distinct overlapping cytokinesis.

items.title: Count within cells and poles
items.guide: With 2n=54: a leaf cell after mitotic cytokinesis has 54 unduplicated chromosomes. A haploid gametophyte after S has 27 duplicated chromosomes; S is interphase, not mitosis. At anaphase I before cytokinesis, the whole meiotic cell still contains 54 duplicated chromosomes, with 27 moving toward each pole. State the counting boundary.
items.bindingReview: 2n54: leaf54 unduplicated, gametophyte27 duplicated, wholeanaphaseI54 duplicated/perpole27; source S-of-mitosis wording corrected.

items.title: Connect Mendel to meiosis
items.guide: Segregation follows separation of homologous chromosomes carrying allele pairs. Independent assortment follows independent orientation of different homologous pairs in meiosis I. Linked loci on one chromosome require qualification. Dominance concerns allele effects on phenotype and is not caused merely by chromosome separation.
items.bindingReview: Separate segregation and different-pair orientation; dominance is an expression relationship, linkedloci qualified.

items.title: Distinguish inheritance vocabulary
items.guide: Genotype describes allele constitution; phenotype describes an observed characteristic. Homozygous means the same allele form at a locus; heterozygous means different forms. Under complete dominance, one allele’s effect is expressed in the heterozygote; “dominant” does not mean common, superior or stronger in every biological sense.
items.bindingReview: Both pairs of genotypewords and complete-dominance phenotype relation; no commonness or superiority inference.

items.title: Calculate a specified chromosome combination
items.guide: Ignoring crossing over and assuming independent assortment, choosing the paternal-origin homologue from each of 23 pairs has probability (1/2)²³ = 1/8,388,608. This is one specified combination, not the probability of any viable egg. Crossing over makes real inheritance combinations more varied.
items.bindingReview: 23independent one-half choices give1/8388608 foronespecifiedpaternalset combination.

items.title: Compare exchange and segregation errors
items.guide: For crossing over, draw two duplicated homologues paired at corresponding loci and mark an exchange between two nonsister chromatids. Trace the swapped segments into balanced products. For nondisjunction, start with 2n=4 and show one homologous pair moving together in meiosis I; after meiosis II the four products have 3, 3, 1 and 1 chromosomes instead of the usual 2 each. These unbalanced products are more likely to impair viability than a normal balanced exchange, although the affected chromosome and developmental context matter. Label homologues, sisters, the error stage and each product boundary.
items.bindingReview: Two diagram mechanisms now trace explicit labels and four nondisjunction counts; balanced exchange compared with imbalance.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed omitted requested comparisons, cross possibilities, procedures or concrete model responses.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Crossing over exchanges corresponding segments between nonsister homologous chromatids and normally increases combinations. Nondisjunction fails to separate chromosomes properly and can create aneuploid products. Those unbalanced products are more likely to impair viability, although outcomes depend on the specific change.

items.title: Compare human and fern cycles
items.guide: Humans have a multicellular diploid body and haploid gametes, with meiosis in gamete formation. Typical ferns have diploid sporophytes and multicellular haploid gametophytes: meiosis makes spores, mitosis makes gametes, and fertilization restores diploidy. Human internal fertilization and development protect gametes or early offspring from some external conditions but require substantial parental resources. Fern spores can disperse to new sites and the gametophyte can grow independently, but typical fern sperm need water to reach the egg. Both sexual cycles reshuffle inherited variants. Compare protection, dispersal and environmental dependence rather than ranking one as universally better.
items.bindingReview: Plant versus animal ploidy transitions and specific benefits/trade-offs now explicit; optional external-dependence context supplied.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source review completed omitted requested comparisons, cross possibilities, procedures or concrete model responses.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Humans have a multicellular diploid stage and haploid gametes; meiosis forms gametes. Ferns have multicellular diploid sporophytes and haploid gametophytes; meiosis forms spores and mitosis forms gametes. Compare dispersal, dependence on water for fertilization in typical ferns, and opportunities for variation without calling one cycle universally better.

items.preAttemptContext: In typical ferns, spores can disperse and grow into a haploid gametophyte; motile sperm depend on water to reach an egg. Human fertilization and prenatal development occur internally and require substantial biological support. These features provide context for comparing protection, dispersal and environmental dependence.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Connect classical and molecular accounts
items.guide: Classically, alleles segregate and unlinked traits assort independently; dominance describes heterozygote phenotype. Molecularly, alleles are DNA variants carried on chromosomes, chromosome behaviour explains transmission, and gene products/regulation help explain phenotype. Not every trait follows a one-gene complete-dominance model.
items.bindingReview: Allclassical/molecular dimensions linked: discretefactors, chromosome transmission, geneproducts andexpression, not universal onegene.

items.title: Calculate F1 and F2
items.guide: WW × ww gives all Ww normal-winged F1. Crossing F1 heterozygotes gives 1 WW:2 Ww:1 ww and, under complete dominance, 3 normal:1 short. Distinguish genotype from phenotype ratios and state that these are expected probabilities.
items.bindingReview: WW×ww allWw; F1cross1:2:1 genotype,3:1 phenotype.

items.guide: A is transcription from DNA to RNA. B is translation of an mRNA sequence into a polypeptide. RNA is made by complementary base pairing; translation uses codons, tRNAs and ribosomes. DNA does not move bodily into the protein.

items.guide: mRNA provides codons, tRNA links codon recognition to amino-acid delivery, and rRNA contributes ribosomal structure and catalysis. The adaptor anticodon belongs to tRNA. A stop codon is recognized through termination machinery, not a tRNA carrying a “stop amino acid”.

items.title: Define biotechnology tools
items.guide: Restriction enzymes cut at recognition sites. A DNA microarray uses known probes to compare hybridization patterns for many sequences. A vector carries a DNA insert into a biological system. Recombinant DNA joins sequences into a new arrangement. These tools produce different evidence and do not by themselves guarantee successful expression.

items.preAttemptContext: A DNA microarray contains many known nucleic-acid probes at identified positions. Complementary sample material can bind, producing a pattern used to compare represented sequences or, with suitable preparation, gene-expression signals. Binding measures a match under the assay conditions; it does not directly prove a functional effect.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Distinguish segregation from assortment
items.guide: For a diploid plant with 2n=4 and genotype Ss at one locus, S and s segregate so each normal gamete receives one. Independent assortment describes this chromosome pair’s orientation relative to the other pair; it is not a second name for separating S from s. Label homologues and the second pair in the diagram.

items.title: Qualify inheritance in asexual organisms
items.guide: In a lineage that reproduces by division, a mutation in the cell giving rise to offspring may be transmitted directly. In a multicellular asexual organism, inheritance still depends on whether the altered cell contributes to a new individual. “Somatic” and “germ line” are not interchangeable in every reproductive system.

items.title: Use predictable DNA cuts
items.guide: Sequence recognition and reproducible cleavage allow a restriction enzyme to generate known fragments. Some cuts leave compatible overhangs useful for assembly. Explain where ligase is needed to seal the backbone and avoid claiming every cut gives sticky ends.

items.title: Explain gel migration
items.guide: DNA’s phosphate backbone is negatively charged, so fragments move toward the positive electrode. Within a suitable gel and comparison, smaller fragments generally travel farther than larger fragments because they pass through the matrix more readily. A ladder is needed to estimate size.

items.preAttemptContext: DNA’s phosphate backbone carries negative charge under standard electrophoresis conditions. An electric field attracts it toward the positive electrode, while the gel matrix impedes fragments according to size and other experimental conditions.

items.title: Test a universal ploidy claim
items.guide: The statement is false. A somatic diploid cell can remain diploid through its mitotic cycle; replication changes DNA amount, not ploidy. Haploid phases belong to specified life cycles and cell lineages, not necessarily every individual cell.

items.title: Explain a karyotype
items.guide: A karyotype organizes chromosome images by size, centromere position and band pattern to inspect number and large structural changes. A digital procedure selects a suitable chromosome spread, separates images and groups homologues. It does not read every DNA sequence or diagnose every genetic condition.

items.title: Evaluate a spindle-target claim
items.guide: Preventing spindle attachment can disrupt chromosome segregation and division, so the proposal has a plausible cellular mechanism. It would also affect other dividing cells and may not stop every tumour pathway. Cell evidence alone does not establish a safe or effective cancer treatment.

items.title: Compare breeding and engineering
items.guide: Selection can breed individuals showing heritable cold tolerance across generations. Engineering could introduce or alter a justified sequence, followed by expression and performance testing. Breeding uses existing variation but may be slow; engineering can target a known mechanism but needs evidence about regulation, unintended effects and environmental performance. Neither guarantees an Alberta-adapted lemon.

items.title: Explain environmental regulation
items.guide: A change in gene expression can alter developmental pathways without replacing the whole genome. One hypothesis is that a female-associated waterborne cue inhibits the male-to-female transition; its absence permits an expression change. A proposed study could compare matched replicated groups with a female present, no female, and no female but water conditioned by females, while holding food, density, temperature and timing comparable. Track individuals, survival, transition timing and a proposed expression marker. If the cue hypothesis is correct, absence should increase transitions and conditioned water should reduce that increase. Contact effects or other differences remain alternatives. This tests a species-specific hypothesis; it is not an established mechanism or a general claim about human development.

items.guide: Ultrasound can identify some anatomical signs; targeted genetic analysis of an appropriately obtained sample can test a particular variant. items.title: Compare genomes and expression
items.guide: Brain and liver cells generally share the same inherited DNA profile at the usual tested loci even though they express different genes. Somatic mutations, mosaicism and assay limits qualify “exactly the same.” Different cell functions do not require wholly different inherited genomes.

items.guide: A defensible model connects exposure to mutagens → DNA damage/repair outcomes → possible mutations in growth-control pathways → altered cell survival/division → clonal expansion with additional changes. Smoking raises risk but does not make cancer inevitable, and one diagram cannot diagnose a tumour or identify all its causes.

items.title: Plan an explanatory presentation
items.guide:
Key message: A mutation is a genetic sequence change. Its effects and transmission depend on the sequence, cell lineage and conditions, so a changed base alone does not predict a person’s future.

Introduction — 1. Define DNA as information stored in base order. A gene is a region used to produce a functional product. 2. Define mutation as sequence change. Distinguish it from a new combination of unchanged parental alleles. 3. State the evidence question. Separate a molecular observation from an inferred whole-organism effect.

Sources and types — 1. Copying can introduce mismatches. Proofreading and repair correct many, so not every initial error persists. 2. Mutagens can raise change frequency under particular conditions. Compare exposed and reference models using the same measurement method. 3. Substitution replaces a base; insertion adds and deletion removes sequence. Place original and changed sequences side by side to show the actual operation.

Sequence to function — 1. GAA and GAG both encode glutamate in the standard RNA code. This illustrates a synonymous change, not proof of no possible RNA effect. 2. A missense change replaces one amino acid. Position and protein function determine whether the effect is small or substantial. 3. Adding one base inside a coding frame can regroup later triplets. A change outside that translated region is not automatically a protein frameshift.

Inheritance and evidence — 1. A body-cell mutation can pass to daughter cells in that lineage. It usually does not reach sexual offspring unless the gamete lineage is involved. 2. Sequence, RNA, protein and cell behaviour are different evidence levels. A claim about function needs more than a sequence difference alone. 3. A variant can be harmful, neutral or beneficial under different conditions. Organisms do not generate a useful mutation because they foresee a need.

Conclusion — 1. Revisit the fictional sequence examples. Identify both the immediate prediction and its limitation. 2. State the next observation that would test a functional claim. Matched controls and replication make that comparison stronger. 3. End with respectful communication. Explain uncertainty and use fictional cases rather than requesting private health or family information.
items.bindingReview: Now includes actualkeymessage and fiveheadings withthreeexplainedpoints each, as requested; no placeholderdirections.

Under each, give a definition, a specific example and a misconception correction. Use fictional sequences and avoid personal health predictions.

items.title: Evaluate a transgene claim
items.guide: The finding raises a question about movement of a recombinant construct or contamination, not proof that corn can naturally cross with any weed. Verify sequence identity, sampling controls and reproductive compatibility. Two possible discussion points for each fictional interview are: farmer—whether weed control still works, and added management cost; developer—evidence tracing the construct, and monitoring or containment responsibilities; organic neighbour—possible effects on nearby crops, and costs of detection or separation; consumer group—transparency of evidence, and access to meaningful choices; genetics researcher—the transfer mechanism, and alternative explanations such as contamination. These are proposed interview topics, not quotations or claims that every stakeholder shares them. Separate measured findings from values and unresolved mechanisms.

Do not assume corn naturally crosses with any unrelated weed. items.title: Evaluate experimental design history
items.guide: Peas offered controlled pollination, many offspring and distinguishable traits. Cats have longer generation times, fewer offspring and more difficult controlled breeding, so patterns could have been harder to infer. This changes the evidence available, not the underlying chromosome mechanisms.

items.title: Apply genetics to conservation
items.guide: Two specific uses are choosing breeding pairs using relatedness evidence to avoid repeatedly pairing close relatives, and comparing genetic variation among source and release populations when planning which lineages to retain. These can help preserve variation and test compatibility with a conservation goal. Neither guarantees recovery: habitat, behaviour, survival and later reproduction also need evidence and monitoring.

revisionHistory.previousGuide: Genetic evidence can help avoid excessive relatedness in planned breeding and preserve variation across a population. It can also help identify population structure for release planning. Genetic diversity alone does not establish habitat suitability, behaviour or long-term recovery; include those evidence needs.

items.title: Connect technology and discovery
items.guide: Three examples are advances in optics and staining making chromosomes easier to distinguish, X-ray diffraction providing structural constraints on DNA, and computing enabling comparison of large sequence datasets. A possible future advance is a less damaging, higher-resolution live-cell imaging method that could follow replication or chromosome movement for longer. That is a proposed capability: it would need validation that the observation method does not itself substantially change the process being studied.

A proposed future technology should name the observation it would improve and the question it would help answer, rather than simply promising faster discovery.

items.title: Compare genetics and genomics
items.guide: Genetics studies inheritance and gene function, often at selected loci; genomics examines genomes and broader patterns across many regions. A genetics study could test whether a particular variant changes an enzyme’s function, helping explain an inherited mechanism. A genomics study could compare many crop genomes to identify candidate regions associated with drought response, then test those candidates. These can benefit health knowledge or agriculture, but association, function and successful application require separate evidence; privacy and access also matter.

revisionHistory.previousGuide: Genetics studies inheritance and gene function, often at particular loci; genomics examines genomes and their broader relationships. A single-variant inheritance study and a genome-wide comparison can answer different questions. Both can support health or conservation research, with interpretation and privacy limits.

items.preAttemptContext: Genomics examines whole genomes or broad patterns across many genomic regions. Genetics includes inheritance and gene function, often studied at particular loci. The fields overlap; their names do not automatically determine which evidence is needed.

items.title: Reject a deterministic premise
items.guide: The premise of one validated gene for high IQ is unsupported: complex cognitive traits depend on many variants, development, environment and how they are measured. If an unvalidated intervention were marketed, possible social effects include unequal access and discrimination based on misunderstood genetic predictions. A proposed research policy could require convincing evidence, independent ethical review, safeguards for children, transparent reporting and no clinical enhancement claims without demonstrated safety and benefit. Preparatory steps could include public education about complex traits, privacy protections and discussion with affected communities. These are reasoned policy proposals, not statements of current law or proof that the intervention works.

items.title: Justify a funding model
items.guide: One defensible example allocates $30 million to transgenic-crop research, $35 million to somatic gene-therapy research and $35 million to cell-cycle research, totalling $100 million. Crop work could examine food-production benefits alongside ecological effects; somatic therapy could test delivery and functional benefit; cell-cycle work could improve basic understanding of growth regulation. Apply the same criteria—evidence quality, likely benefit, uncertainty, access and sustainability—to each programme. Fund clear milestones, publish limitations and revise later allocations when evidence changes. Other splits can be justified; the example is a reasoned allocation, not a uniquely correct answer.

A valid response explains trade-offs and monitoring; there is no uniquely correct numerical split.

items.title: Compare benefits and risks across levels
items.guide: A conditional comparison table could read: individuals—possible increased organ availability versus rejection, infection and uncertain function; society—possible reduced waiting burden versus unequal access and welfare concerns; economy—possible reduction of some long-term care costs versus research, breeding and monitoring costs; other species—possible knowledge relevant to animal health versus direct burdens on donor animals; environment—no direct benefit demonstrated by this scenario versus resource use, waste and containment demands. Each proposed benefit requires evidence. The exercise evaluates a research scenario, not current clinical safety, availability or legal status.

items.title: Explain shared molecular principles
items.guide: Different organisms share conserved molecular features, so experiments in varied systems can reveal general DNA mechanisms. Complementary evidence can strengthen a model, but organism-specific differences and exceptions still matter. A successful result in one system does not automatically establish every application in another.

items.title: Separate empirical and philosophical claims
items.guide: A reasoned paragraph may connect heredity, metabolism, replication and regulation to questions about life, then discuss limits raised by viruses, artificial constructs or cloning. Distinguish testable biological observations from a personal philosophical conclusion and acknowledge a contrasting interpretation.
